text:
Jet fuel demand in India would rise from about 192,000 barrels per day in 2024 to 277,000 barrels per day by 2031, providing a strong market for the Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), as per a report released on Monday.

The government has announced SAF blending roadmap starting with 1 per cent blending in 2027 and increasing to 2 per cent in 2028 and 5 per cent in 2030 to decarbonise the aviation industry.

The report jointly developed by S&P Global Energy and the SAF Association estimates that the SAF demand will be 46,000 tonne in 2027, which would rise to 250,000 tonne in 2030.

India's aviation sector is expected to remain one of the fastest-growing sources of refined product demand through 2060, providing a strong foundation for developing a domestic SAF market, the report said.

"This expansion is driven by rising middle-class mobility, continued growth in domestic and international air travel, airport infrastructure development, and ongoing airline fleet additions," it said.

The report, released at 2nd India SAF Conclave, noted that while some short-term weakness emerged in 2026, particularly in the international segment, the underlying demand trajectory remains firmly positive.

India's aviation fuel consumption softened in mid-2026, with July demand falling to about 180,000 barrel per day reflecting weaker flight activity, higher operating costs, and supply-side disruptions, it said.

However, first-half 2026 jet fuel consumption still increased by nearly 2 per cent year-over-year, suggesting the recent slowdown is temporary rather than structural and does not alter the longer-term growth outlook, the report said.

"The demand outlook is further supported by rising passenger traffic, the continued expansion of low-cost aviation, and increasing international connectivity," it said.

New infrastructure, including Navi Mumbai International Airport and Jewar Airport in Noida, is expected to ease capacity constraints and support additional growth in flight activity.

International aviation is likely to remain an important demand driver, with international seat capacity expanding faster than domestic capacity in 2026 despite higher ticket costs.

"Policy support is also expected to play an important role in sustaining aviation growth. A key structural driver is the government's continued focus on expanding air connectivity through UDAN (Ude Desh Ka Aam Nagrik) Regional Connectivity Scheme," the report said.

It highlighted that the government has introduced an aviation turbine fuel (ATF) pricing stabilization mechanism, including a fixed ATF price in Delhi and a dedicated stabilization fund.

While not a direct subsidy, the mechanism reduces fuel price volatility and improves cost visibility for airlines, it added.

title: 300MW electrolyser construction starts off Spanish 'hydrogen valley' - Chemistry World
authors: Andy Extance, Rosie Rothwell, Phillip Broadwith, Julia Robinson, Mason Wakley, Maria Burke, Anthony King, Victoria Atkinson, Rebecca Trager
description:
In September, Spanish energy company Moeve started building a 300MW solar-powered electrolyser to make CO2-emission-free ‘green’ hydrogen in Huelva, in the south of the country.
This is billed as the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve has ambitions to develop to a total electrolysis capacity of 2GW.
Odenweller’s research highlights ‘ambition gaps’ between announcements about green hydrogen and reality, with many projects being abandoned.
He highlights that the Huelva plant is set to produce 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually.
Odenweller expects green hydrogen demand from the plant to remain clustered within the nearby hydrogen valley region ‘for the foreseeable future’.
text:
In September, Spanish energy company Moeve started building a 300MW solar-powered electrolyser to make CO2-emission-free ‘green’ hydrogen in Huelva, in the south of the country. The Spanish government is contributing €300 million (£260 million) towards the over €1 billion cost of the site. Moeve intends to use the hydrogen to replace some of the fossil-derived hydrogen it uses at the existing refinery onsite, as well as hydrogenating waste vegetable oils to make low-emissions liquid hydrocarbon fuels for aviation, shipping and heavy-duty road transport, and in chemical manufacturing.

This is billed as the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve has ambitions to develop to a total electrolysis capacity of 2GW. It follows similar projects in Lingen, Germany, where RWE intends to have a 300GW electrolyser operational next year, and Stegra’s 700GW plant that – once commissioned – will feed green iron and steel production in Boden, Sweden.

Adrian Odenweller from Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, Germany, calls starting to build such a large project ‘encouraging’, although there are several larger projects worldwide. ‘This project may be particularly important for Europe, to demonstrate the feasibility of producing hydrogen in renewable-rich regions such as the Iberian Peninsula, co-located with demand,’ he says.

Odenweller’s research highlights ‘ambition gaps’ between announcements about green hydrogen and reality, with many projects being abandoned. He highlights that the Huelva plant is set to produce 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually. This is only 0.45% the EU’s target for 2030, which Odenweller says ‘is clearly out of reach by now’.

Nevertheless, the project ‘is certainly an important building block in Spain and Europe’s clean hydrogen market,’ says Peter Collins, a spokesperson for industry group Hydrogen Europe. ‘The scale and significance of the project is clear for all to see, and the construction announcement shows what a strong developer can achieve – and how these ambition gaps can be closed – with clear policy frameworks and government support.’

Moeve will use a combination of dedicated solar power generation and electricity from the grid to run the plant. To produce 45,000 tonnes of hydrogen annually from a 300MW electrolysis plant would involve running it for around 7000 hours per year, Odenweller says. That will either require a very large solar plant with electricity storage to smooth out uneven generation, or taking significant electricity from the grid. Odenweller notes that from 2030 onwards, EU Renewable Fuel of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO) rules will allow hydrogen production from grid energy to be classified as green through hourly matching of consumption with renewable power.

Odenweller expects green hydrogen demand from the plant to remain clustered within the nearby hydrogen valley region ‘for the foreseeable future’. Among the potential markets, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is profitable due to relatively limited supply and government mandates for increased use, allowing for premium prices that cover the higher production costs.

Six equipment items already in stock, together with the associated engineering: 75% of the €3.2 million to be received within 30 days of a delivery scheduled before the end of 2026, with no significant industrial cash outlay;

A majority of the revenue to be recognised in the current financial year;

INCAD: the first in a network of some twenty Multi-Energy Hubs in Quebec.

Vitry-le-François, France - 28 September 2026, 08:00 am (CEST)

Haffner Energy announces the signing of a contract for a firm ,3.2 million order with INCAD (Centre d'Intégration de CArburants Durables), the project company responsible for developing the first Multi-Energy Hub in Bécancour, at the heart of Quebec's Energy Transition Valley.

Effective upon signature on 25 September 2026, the contract covers six equipment items already manufactured and available in stock, together with the associated engineering services. The project's remaining equipment will be manufactured in Canada under licence from Haffner Energy.

A compressed payment schedule

The contract provides for a €480,000 down payment, representing 15% of the total amount, due no later than 12 October 2026. Within thirty days of FOB delivery of the equipment, 75% of the contract price will have been invoiced and received.

Delivery is scheduled before the end of 2026, subject to international transport and logistics constraints. This will allow work to bring the equipment into compliance with Canadian standards to begin immediately.

A rapid contribution to cash flow, revenue and earnings

As the six items of equipment to be exported will be drawn from Haffner Energy's existing inventory, their manufacturing costs have already been incurred and paid. Fulfilment of the order will therefore generate rapid cash inflows without any significant new industrial cash outlay.

As revenue is recognised on a percentage-of-completion basis, based on costs incurred, the allocation to the contract of this already-manufactured equipment is expected to enable a majority of the contract revenue to be recognised in the current financial year, with a corresponding contribution to earnings.

An order complementing the licence agreement for the Canadian market

The contract announced today is legally and economically separate from the licence agreement entered into with Mundi Énergies. This agreement covers the deployment of Haffner Energy's technology across the entire Canadian market, beyond the INCAD project alone. In this respect, Haffner Energy has already received an initial licence payment (upfront fee) of €1 million and, in consideration for the licence, holds a 49% stake in Mundi Haffner Technologies Inc., the company responsible for developing the technology in Quebec.

INCAD: the first project in a large-scale Canadian programme

Located in the Bécancour Industrial and Port Park, at the heart of Quebec's Energy Transition Valley, INCAD is developing the first Multi-Energy Hub resulting from the partnership between Haffner Energy and Mundi Énergies. The INCAD unit is designed to produce primarily 400 Nm³/h of renewable natural gas (RNG) from residual biomass. Commissioning is scheduled for the second quarter of 2028.

The site will also produce biochar, which can notably be used as a soil amendment. Biochar contributes to soil regeneration and enables the long-term sequestration of approximately three times its own weight in CO2 equivalent.

A portion of the thermolysis oil produced will be reserved for demonstration campaigns for the production of renewable diesel and renewable aviation fuel, with a view to qualifying the SB-HEFA process for the production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF),

INCAD will thus demonstrate, on an industrial scale, Haffner Energy technology's ability to convert a single resource into RNG, biochar and liquid fuels.

INCAD is the first in a network of some twenty Multi-Energy Hubs that Haffner Energy and Mundi Énergies plan to develop progressively across Quebec. Subsequent projects will target significantly higher capacities. For Haffner Energy, this model combines several revenue streams: sales of proprietary equipment, engineering, licence royalties, maintenance and operations, local manufacturing under licence and minority stakes in project companies.

Mundi Énergies and Haffner Energy prepare the next stages of deployment

The order was signed during the third visit to France by a Mundi Énergies delegation since summer 2025. Comprising Lilianne Trudel, Christian Blais and Sylvain Perreault, the team was able to see Haffner Energy's H6 equipment in operation at the Marolles site.

Sylvain Perreault, President of Mundi Énergies, said:

"Our engineering team had already been very favourably impressed by the H4 generation in July 2025. Having both the H4 equipment and the new H6 generation at the same site provides a particularly compelling illustration of the progress achieved by Haffner Energy, notably in terms of simplification and industrial design. We were also able to see the H6 in operation for the first time.

The modularity of the H6 solution represents a decisive advantage for us. In a country such as Canada, where winters are extremely harsh and the various phases of on-site work have to be organised taking into account weather-related uncertainties and long distances, the ability to produce factory-pretested modules provides much greater control over project schedules and significantly reduces execution risks.

This third visit to France since summer 2025 has enabled us to see very concretely the progress achieved by Haffner Energy and to prepare, together with its teams, the next stages of the INCAD project in Bécancour. It has also enabled us to make significant progress on the deployment of future Multi-Energy Hubs, with several strategic sites currently moving beyond the feasibility-study stage and towards securing their biomass supply."

Philippe Haffner, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Haffner Energy, said:

"Beyond its very significant contribution to the Company's earnings and cash position, this firm order marks a new phase for Haffner Energy. Following several financial years devoted to innovation and to broadening our value proposition beyond hydrogen alone, during which revenue remained very limited, we are now entering the tangible phase of orders, deliveries and deployment, fully returning to the pace of an industrial company, with revenue set to accelerate very sharply from this year onwards.

The order from Mundi Énergies provides our shareholders with a tangible and quantifiable demonstration of our strategy: our strategic equipment and engineering expertise, combined with local manufacturing under licence, within a replicable model. As it monetises equipment already held in inventory, it directly strengthens our cash position.

The technical and industrial success of the H6, which our partners saw operating in Marolles, confirms the simplification of our platform. H6 technology is paving the way for the next projects in Quebec, which will have significantly greater capacities, as well as for our large-scale industrial deployment through the CORE100 programme.

Finally, INCAD will serve as an industrial and commercial showcase for Canada and North America: a single site producing RNG and biochar, while demonstrating our pathway to renewable diesel and, ultimately, SAF."

About Haffner Energy

Haffner Energy designs and supplies innovative solutions for the production of competitive renewable fuels from biomass. With over 33 years' experience using all types of biomass, the company has developed proprietary thermolysis and gasification technologies enabling the production of renewable gas, hydrogen, renewable methanol, power, and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

As well as supplying technology, Haffner Energy supports its clients in developing industrial projects designed to accelerate the decarbonization of the energy, industrial and transport sectors. Its solutions also contribute to the production of biogenic CO2 and biochar, thereby supporting the energy transition and the sustainable use of biomass.

New Delhi [India], September 28 (ANI): As India expands rapidly across the aviation landscape, Ambassador of Iceland to India, Bendikt Hoskuldsson, stated that the time to bring solutions for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to the table is now and not in the distant future. He highlighted that this can only happen by partnering with different stakeholders.

Speaking to ANI on the sidelines of the India SAF Conclave 2026, the Ambassador stressed that collaborative efforts remain essential for decarbonising air travel and advancing clean aviation technologies.

“India is the fastest-growing market in the world. You are the biggest populous country in the world. So your aviation industry is going to move and grow really fast. So the time to bring the solutions to the table is now. They're not in the distant future; they're now. So, but that only happens through partnering with different stakeholders such as us and others,” Hoskuldsson said.

He also shared that Iceland’s national carrier, Icelandair, is already carrying out trials to produce SAF for its fleet and seeking to scale up operational adoption. He stated that while one nation's model cannot be replicated entirely, shared technical expertise helps address localised requirements.

“We don't have solutions that you can copy-paste. That's not how we approach this. We approach this as you have different tasks, you have different challenges, and we can bring our experiences and expertise to those,” he said.

He noted that Iceland’s clean technology capabilities, particularly around carbon capture, utilisation, and storage, provide a viable pathway for producing sustainable fuels. He explained that commercial experience in this segment can aid international partners seeking alternatives.

“Iceland has already achieved quite a lot of the goals that we have set in terms of addressing the climate issues that we have as a country. I think the biggest issue, when it comes to aviation fuel is, you know, there are different ways that you can reach e-methanols or e-fuels. What we are offering is the carbon capture, use and storage technologies. We've been doing it commercially for over 20 years,” he said.

The Ambassador underlined that bilateral economic mechanisms provide an immediate framework for such engagements. He referenced the trade pact between India and the four-nation European Free Trade Association, which includes Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein, and Switzerland, as a vehicle to tap joint industrial opportunities.

“We have to bring together the right stakeholders to address this issue. And so what we can do is we can bring our experiences which are over 20 years old in this space and we stand ready to do that,” Hoskuldsson said. (ANI)

CUPERTINO, Calif., Sept. 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aemetis, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMTX), a diversified renewable natural gas and biofuels company, today announced that it has received $22.4 million from the sale of Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Tax Credits.

The Section 45Z tax credits were generated from ethanol and renewable natural gas (RNG) production in 2026 and represent a tax credit value of approximately $0.33 per gallon of ethanol and $62 per MMBtu of RNG, before sale discounts and transaction costs. The tax credit value is based on the recent update to the 45ZCF-GREET model that was issued by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) on September 8, 2026.

"Aemetis continues to benefit from Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Tax Credits as a recurring source of cash flow, executing on our monetization strategy," said Eric McAfee, Chairman and CEO of Aemetis. "With recent updates this month to the Section 45Z calculation and expected expansion of production volumes and energy efficiency projects, the ongoing value of Section 45Z credits to Aemetis is expected to continue to grow significantly."

The new September 8 version of the 45ZCF-GREET model includes updated pathways for RNG produced from dairy manure anaerobic digestion as required by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. It also now allows ethanol producers to account for low-carbon corn feedstock that is grown with regenerative agricultural practices. Aemetis expects to increase the value per gallon of its ethanol Section 45Z credit once the use of low-carbon corn is fully documented.

"We appreciate the work by Treasury, the IRS, DOE, and USDA to release the update to the 45ZCF-GREET calculations in compliance with the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act," added McAfee. Moeve and Emerita Resources have signed the first agreement in Spain to deploy 100% renewable diesel (HVO) on an industrial scale within the mining sector. Through this partnership, Moeve has positioned itself as the preferred supplier of this 2G biofuel, which can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 90% over its entire life cycle compared to traditional diesel.

This 2G biofuel is produced at Moeve’s facility in Palos de la Frontera (Huelva) and will be implemented in the operations of the Iberian Belt West (IBW) project, led by Emerita Resources and located in the province of Huelva, between the towns of Puebla de Guzmán and Paymogo. Specifically, it will be used both in the heavy machinery employed for construction and operations at the complex and in the heavy-duty transport of concentrates. In addition to being key to decarbonizing sectors that are difficult to electrify—such as air, maritime, and heavy-duty road transport—the main added value of using HVO lies in its compatibility with current engines.

The use of this biofuel in transportation operations during the mine’s construction and operation is estimated to prevent the emission of approximately 2,600 metric tons of CO2 annually—a reduction equivalent to the annual carbon absorption of 170,000 trees—which would allow a truck to travel a distance of three million kilometers.

"Accelerating the decarbonization of heavy industry is one of Moeve’s key strategic priorities, and to achieve this, we need forward-thinking partners. The agreement reached with Emerita demonstrates that the energy transition can go hand in hand with competitiveness by leveraging 2G biofuels as an immediate solution for the decarbonization of sectors that are difficult to electrify.”

text:
Australian technology company Hazer Group has reported independent testing indicating its graphite can replace part of petroleum-derived bitumen in heavy-duty asphalt while maintaining or improving key performance characteristics.

The testing, conducted by Boral Construction Materials Technical Services, assessed Hazer graphite in several dense-graded asphalt formulations commonly used in road construction. The formulations were tested against Transport for New South Wales specifications for heavy-duty pavement applications, according to Hazer.

In an ASX announcement, Hazer said the testing found graphite-containing asphalt met applicable performance requirements while improving several durability and engineering measures.

One formulation containing Hazer graphite recorded a Tensile Strength Ratio of 89%, compared with 81% for the conventional control mix. Hazer said the result indicated improved resistance to moisture-related damage and stripping.

The company also reported improvements in tensile strength across graphite-containing formulations, as well as resistance to rutting and deformation. Testing further indicated improved ageing characteristics compared with conventional asphalt binders.

Hazer CEO and Managing Director Glenn Corrie said the results provided further evidence of the potential applications for the company’s graphite in infrastructure markets.

“These latest results represent an important step forward in demonstrating the functional performance and versatility of Hazer graphite in large-scale infrastructure applications,” Corrie said.

Hazer said the results could support the use of its graphite as a lower-emissions additive to partially replace petroleum-derived bitumen. However, the company noted that any environmental benefits from the substitution would require further lifecycle assessment and validation.

The company is targeting the global bitumen market, with Hazer estimating demand in road construction and pavement at about 122 million tonnes per year. It cited reported spot prices of US$383 to US$724 per tonne across major international ports as a reference range for the potential value of graphite as a partial replacement material.

Hazer said asphalt applications form part of a broader graphite commercialisation strategy covering high-volume markets including steelmaking and cement, alongside potential higher-value applications.

Выпуск авиатоплива в Казахстане по итогам года составит 825 тысяч тонн – Минэнерго

Это на 13% больше показателя 2025 года

28.09.2026 · 09:20

За восемь месяцев этого года в Казахстане произвели 591 тыс. тонн авиатоплива, передает центр деловой информации Kapital.kz со ссылкой на пресс-службу министерства энергетики.

«Министерство энергетики проводит постоянную работу по увеличению производства авиатоплива и обеспечению внутреннего рынка. Согласно плану, в 2026 году было намечено производство 750 тыс. тонн авиатоплива. При этом за восемь месяцев уже произведено 591 тыс. тонн. По итогам года ожидается выпуск 825 тыс. тонн, что на 13% больше, чем в прошлом году. Для сравнения: в 2025 году произвели 726 тыс. тонн», - привели данные в отраслевом ведомстве.

Как ожидают в министерстве, в дальнейшем производство будет последовательно увеличиваться и к 2031 году планируется довести его до 1,5 млн тонн.

В Минэнерго подчеркивают, что потребности казахстанской гражданской авиации, структур силового блока, гражданской защиты и госматрезерва полностью покрываются отечественным авиатопливом. Ежегодная внутренняя потребность пассажирской авиации составляет 680 тыс. тонн.

Ранее стало известно, что в Туркестанской области построят базу хранения авиатоплива за 19 млрд тенге. «КазМунайГаз-Аэро» построит в аэропорту Актобе топливозаправочный комплекс за 5 млрд тенге. «КазМунайГаз-Аэро», KazFoodProducts и американская компания KBR подписали соглашения, открывающие новый этап реализации проекта по строительству первого в Казахстане завода по производству устойчивого авиационного топлива (Sustainable Aviation Fuel, SAF).

Также сообщалось, что Казахстан пока не может полностью закрыть внутренний спрос на авиационное топливо за счет собственного производства: дефицитный объем приходится компенсировать импортом, в том числе из России и других стран.

При работе с материалами Центра деловой информации Kapital.kz разрешено использование лишь 30% текста с обязательной гиперссылкой на источник. При использовании полного материала необходимо разрешение редакции.

description:

Local market Following the recent conclusion of export deals for October and November loading, Argentina’s domestic tallow market responded by holding steady.
Market participants generally agreed that Argentine domestic tallow prices were unlikely to fall significantly under current supply conditions.
Some sellers expected prices to firm, while others said weak local consumption would prevent export-related tightness from translating into a substantial increase in domestic prices.
text:
Fastmarkets assessed tallow, max 5% FFA, fob Argentina at $1,170-1,200 per tonne in the week to Thursday, unchanged from a week earlier.

Fastmarkets assessed common tallow, max 3% FFA, exw Argentina at 1,420,000-1,450,000 Argentine pesos ($934-954) per tonne in the week to Thursday, unchanged from a week earlier.

Meanwhile, prime tallow, max 2% FFA, exw Argentina was assessed at 1,450,000 pesos per tonne in the week to Thursday, also unchanged from a week earlier.

Sources told Fastmarkets that deals for November loading had also been concluded. While some suppliers were attempting to secure shipments for December, other market participants were taking a more cautious approach due to uncertainty surrounding the US market.

“It is a combination of factors, including tariffs on Brazil, elections in Brazil and the United States, supplies from Oceania into the US and US biofuel credit policies. In addition, the decline in Chicago packer tallow prices is curbing the expectations of Argentine exporters seeking higher values,” one source said.

Two market participants pointed to predominantly bullish positioning among investment funds in Chicago soyoil futures, particularly in the December contract.

“The US market outlook is bullish, and prices will rise quickly and significantly. It is just a matter of time,” one of the sources said.

“Open interest in options on the December CBOT soyoil contract has strengthened in recent days, providing a new perspective on prices and potentially creating fresh opportunities for US feedstock buyers in other regions,” the other source said.

Managed money increased its bullish positioning in CBOT soyoil futures and options in the week to September 15, adding 5,230 long lots while reducing short positions by 3,896 lots. This lifted the category’s net-long position by 9,126 lots to 110,894 lots, according to the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Commitments of Traders report. The next report, covering the week to September 22, was scheduled for release on Friday September 25.

Local market

Following the recent conclusion of export deals for October and November loading, Argentina’s domestic tallow market responded by holding steady.

According to sources, household consumption of tallow remained weak, resulting in limited demand from refiners producing edible tallow.

“Because of weak purchasing power and a significant imbalance in relative prices in Argentina, meat consumption and the use of tallow for cooking have been very weak. But because there is no demand, the lack of tallow goes ‘unnoticed’,” one source said.

According to the source, cattle slaughter in Argentina remained very low, although activity had recovered somewhat recently, particularly for export-oriented cattle. Stronger external demand for beef, especially from Europe, was reportedly providing some support to slaughter rates despite weak domestic consumption.

“The beef industry is facing a very challenging environment. Cattle prices are high relative to the economic realities faced by meatpackers. International beef prices are favorable and the domestic market is not performing too badly, but processors’ operating costs are very high. At the same time, returns from by-products such as hides, offal and tallow are negligible,” another source said.

Market participants generally agreed that Argentine domestic tallow prices were unlikely to fall significantly under current supply conditions. Views on the potential for an increase were more mixed, however. Some sellers expected prices to firm, while others said weak local consumption would prevent export-related tightness from translating into a substantial increase in domestic prices.

Several sources said local producers were increasingly monitoring export opportunities, which could offer better returns than domestic sales. Some market participants were reportedly storing material for October, when export commitments could tighten local availability, while renderers with access to international channels were directing more product toward export markets.

title: EU SAF supply exceeds first ReFuelEU target, feedstock reliance remains high: EASA
description:
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) was supplied at 121 Union airports across all 27 EU member states in 2025, equivalent to 79% of EU airports, EASA said.
A further 120,000 tonnes, or around 11%, was classified as other aviation biofuels, while 90,000 tonnes, or about 8%, was advanced aviation biofuels.
Spain received 152,000 tonnes, Germany 116,000 tonnes, Italy 111,000 tonnes and France 107,000 tonnes.
Together, those five countries accounted for about 74% of EU SAF supply.
EASA notes that the aviation biofuel and conventional aviation fuel figures were the only categories for which it could establish a real index price.
text:
Aviation fuel suppliers reported supplying 39.3 million tonnes of aviation fuel to aircraft operators within the scope of ReFuelEU Aviation in 2025, of which SAF accounted for 1.1 million, or 2.79%, according to the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA).

The increase also came alongside a broader expansion in physical availability. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) was supplied at 121 Union airports across all 27 EU member states in 2025, equivalent to 79% of EU airports, EASA said.

UCO remained dominant

The composition of the SAF supplied provides a clearer picture of what drove the increase.

Of the 1.1 million tonnes reported, 885,000 tonnes, or about 80%, was classified as aviation biofuel produced from feedstocks listed under Annex IX Part B of the EU Renewable Energy Directive. A further 120,000 tonnes, or around 11%, was classified as other aviation biofuels, while 90,000 tonnes, or about 8%, was advanced aviation biofuels.

Used cooking oil (UCO) accounted for 80% of the total SAF feedstock mix, broadly unchanged from 81% in 2024.

The remaining 20% included category 3 animal fats at 11%, palm oil mill effluent (POME) at 5%, with food waste, crude tall oil (CTO) and category 1 and 2 animal fats making up the balance.

Synthetic aviation fuel did not contribute to aircraft operators’ reported SAF purchases in 2025, while 69.6% of the 1 million tonnes purchased by aircraft operators was classified as aviation biofuel.

Imported feedstocks dominate the supply chain

EASA found that 85% of the feedstock used to produce the SAF originated outside the EU.

China alone accounted for 61% of feedstock origin, followed by Malaysia at 8%, Indonesia at 5% and the UK at 3%. Only 15% of feedstock originated within the EU.

That means the 2025 data shows a European SAF supply chain that is increasingly capable of processing and supplying SAF domestically, but remains highly exposed to international feedstock flows.

This is particularly relevant for the HEFA market, where UCO, animal fats and other waste-based feedstocks compete across renewable diesel, SAF and other renewable fuel applications.

Voluntary SAF made up almost one-quarter of reported supply

The data also shows that not all of the 1.1 million tonnes reported by suppliers was intended to count toward the ReFuelEU minimum share.

Around 250,000 tonnes was reported as voluntary SAF, meaning it was explicitly identified by suppliers as not counting toward the minimum ReFuelEU share. That volume represented almost one-quarter of total reported SAF supply.

At the same time, EASA cautioned that the reported 1.1 million tonnes could slightly underestimate actual EU SAF supply because around 10% of obligated fuel suppliers did not report SAF volumes, while the reporting system does not capture SAF supplied to non-Union airports.

The Netherlands was the largest destination for SAF supplied in the EU, receiving 320,000 tonnes, or 29% of total reported SAF, the data shows.

Spain received 152,000 tonnes, Germany 116,000 tonnes, Italy 111,000 tonnes and France 107,000 tonnes. Together, those five countries accounted for about 74% of EU SAF supply.

At airport level, Amsterdam Schiphol accounted for 29% of total SAF supplied, followed by Frankfurt at 8% and Paris Charles de Gaulle at 7%.

EU production capacity is sufficient on paper, but project execution matters

EASA’s 2030 capacity assessment provides another important angle. The agency estimates that current operational facilities alone would provide about 1.5 million tonnes per year of SAF capacity by 2030, below the roughly 2.1 million tonnes required to meet the 6% ReFuelEU SAF minimum share, excluding synthetic aviation fuels.

When facilities under construction or that have reached final investment decision (FID) are included, potential capacity rises to 3.7 million tonnes per year.

A broader scenario that includes projects classified as having a high level of credibility puts potential SAF capacity at 5.5 million tonnes per year, plus 600,000 tonnes per year of eSAF capacity.

Demand-side data shows SAF purchases are already substantial

Aircraft operators reported purchasing around 1 million tonnes of SAF in 2025, with 245 operators reporting SAF purchases.

The top 10 operators accounted for approximately half of those purchases. KLM reported the largest volume at 91,786 tonnes, followed by Ryanair at 78,951 tonnes and Transavia at 68,003 tonnes.

Of the SAF purchased by operators, 624,000 tonnes was reported as intended to be claimed under market-based measures. Of that amount, 512,000 tonnes, or 49% of total SAF purchased, was associated with the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS), 90,000 tonnes with the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) and the equivalent of 2% with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).

Another 415,000 tonnes, or 40% of eligible fuel, was not claimed under a market-based measure.

SAF price gap remains significant

EASA also published 2025 reference prices, with aviation biofuels at €1,925 ($2,205) per tonne compared with €640 per tonne for conventional aviation fuel.

That implies a reference-price gap of about €1,285 per tonne, with aviation biofuels priced at roughly three times the conventional fuel reference price.

EASA notes that the aviation biofuel and conventional aviation fuel figures were the only categories for which it could establish a real index price. Other eligible fuel categories were calculated using bottom-up production-cost estimates.

title: Banking Law And Net-Zero Aviation Transition Spain
description:
Banking Law and Net-Zero Aviation Transition in Spain 1.
There is no separate Spanish statute called the “Net-Zero Aviation Banking Law.” The subject arises from the interaction of: Spanish banking and prudential law; EU sustainable-finance legislation; aviation regulation; the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS); sustainable aviation fuel rules; State-aid law; environmental law; and public and private project finance.
What the Aviation Transition Requires Aviation is difficult to decarbonise because conventional aircraft depend heavily on energy-dense liquid fuels.
Relevant Case Law There is no established judicial category called “Net-Zero Aviation Banking Law.” The strongest relevant jurisprudence therefore comes from EU aviation, environmental and State-aid cases.
Conclusion Banking Law and Net-Zero Aviation Transition in Spain is an emerging intersection of prudential banking regulation, aviation law, sustainable finance, environmental regulation and EU State-aid law.
text:
Banking Law and Net-Zero Aviation Transition in Spain

1. Introduction

Banking Law and Net-Zero Aviation Transition in Spain concerns the role of banks, capital markets, public financial institutions and EU financial regulation in funding the transformation of aviation toward substantially lower greenhouse-gas emissions and, ultimately, climate neutrality.

There is no separate Spanish statute called the “Net-Zero Aviation Banking Law.” The subject arises from the interaction of:

Spanish banking and prudential law;

EU sustainable-finance legislation;

aviation regulation;

the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS);

sustainable aviation fuel rules;

State-aid law;

environmental law; and

public and private project finance.

The regulatory environment has become particularly important following Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 — ReFuelEU Aviation. The Regulation requires progressively increasing shares of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF): the minimum started at 2% in 2025 and rises to 70% by 2050, while a separate synthetic-fuel requirement begins at 0.7% in 2030 and rises to 35% by 2050.

For Spanish banks, this transition creates both financing opportunities and financial risks.

2. Spanish Banking-Law Framework

Banks financing aviation projects in Spain remain subject to the ordinary prudential framework.

The central Spanish statute is Law 10/2014 on the organisation, supervision and solvency of credit institutions, supplemented by Royal Decree 84/2015 and applicable EU banking legislation.

Consequently, a loan does not receive special prudential treatment simply because it supports aviation decarbonisation.

A bank financing an airline, airport, SAF production facility or aviation-technology company must still consider:

borrower creditworthiness;

capital requirements;

concentration risk;

liquidity;

collateral;

project risk;

regulatory risk;

environmental risk; and

expected repayment capacity.

Net-zero objectives therefore operate alongside, rather than instead of, prudent banking standards.

3. What the Aviation Transition Requires

Aviation is difficult to decarbonise because conventional aircraft depend heavily on energy-dense liquid fuels.

The transition therefore requires several types of investment.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel

SAF is one of the principal mechanisms contemplated by current EU regulation.

ReFuelEU Aviation covers aviation biofuels, synthetic aviation fuels and certain recycled-carbon fuels, subject to applicable sustainability criteria.

Synthetic Aviation Fuel

Synthetic fuels can be produced using renewable hydrogen and other processes.

They can require substantial investment in:

renewable electricity;

hydrogen production;

fuel synthesis;

industrial facilities;

storage; and

transport infrastructure.

More Efficient Aircraft

Financing can support aircraft replacement and technologies that reduce fuel consumption.

Airport Infrastructure

Airports may require infrastructure enabling access to SAF and, over the longer term, other lower-emission energy systems.

ReFuelEU Aviation specifically requires EU airport managing bodies to facilitate aircraft operators' access to SAF.

4. ReFuelEU Aviation and Bank Finance

Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 significantly changes the economic environment in which aviation investments are financed.

Fuel suppliers serving Union airports must meet progressively increasing SAF requirements.

The minimum SAF share follows this trajectory:

2025 — 2%

2030 — 6%

2035 — 20%

2040 — 34%

2045 — 42%

2050 — 70%

A separate synthetic aviation fuel component also increases progressively from 2030.

For lenders, legally mandated demand can affect the commercial assessment of projects producing eligible fuels.

A bank considering financing a SAF production facility can therefore examine regulatory demand alongside production costs, supply contracts, technology and feedstock availability.

5. EU Emissions Trading System

Aviation is also covered by the EU ETS.

The system places a carbon cost on covered aviation emissions and is increasingly moving toward the polluter-pays principle.

Free aviation allowances are being phased out, with full auctioning applying in 2026 under the current framework.

At the same time, up to 20 million allowances are reserved for 2024–2030 to help aircraft operators address part of the price difference between eligible sustainable aviation fuels and conventional fossil kerosene. The mechanism is estimated at around €1.6 billion.

This matters to banks because carbon costs can affect:

airline operating expenses;

profitability;

aircraft valuations;

fuel contracts;

financing models; and

long-term creditworthiness.

Climate regulation therefore becomes a conventional credit-risk consideration.

6. Financing SAF Production

One of the largest financing needs arises before fuel reaches an aircraft.

SAF production facilities can require substantial capital expenditure.

Banks may finance:

biorefineries;

renewable-hydrogen facilities;

synthetic-fuel plants;

storage terminals;

renewable-energy infrastructure; and

fuel-distribution systems.

The economic model can combine commercial lending with EIB or other public financing.

The European Investment Bank's approach illustrates how public development finance can complement commercial banks and capital markets when financing low-carbon fuel infrastructure.

For Spain, similar financing principles can support the development of domestic aviation-transition infrastructure.

7. Public and EIB Financing

Public financial institutions can reduce financing barriers for large transition projects.

Spain's Recovery and Resilience framework includes EIB-managed financial instruments capable of supporting sectors including renewable energy, clean transport and sustainable infrastructure.

This does not mean every aviation project automatically qualifies.

Eligibility depends upon the specific financing instrument, project characteristics and applicable EU requirements.

Nevertheless, blended structures can potentially combine:

commercial bank debt + public financing + sponsor equity + EU financial support.

This can be important where transition projects involve high initial investment and long repayment periods.

8. Aerospace Research and Development

The transition also requires technological innovation.

In June 2026, the European Investment Bank announced a €3 billion financing envelope for Airbus research and development, including activities in Spain, France and Germany. A first €1 billion loan was signed under that envelope.

This illustrates a broader principle.

Transition finance does not have to be limited to buying sustainable fuel. It can also finance the technologies and industrial capacity required for future aviation.

9. Transition Risk

A Spanish bank financing aviation must consider transition risk.

Suppose a bank provides a long-term loan to an airline operating relatively inefficient aircraft.

During the life of the loan:

carbon prices may change;

SAF obligations may increase;

fuel prices may change;

aircraft technology may improve; and

customers may alter travel preferences.

The borrower's future costs may therefore differ considerably from historical costs.

A prudent lender can incorporate those factors into cash-flow and stress-testing assumptions.

10. Physical Climate Risk

Aviation infrastructure can also face physical climate risks.

Airports may be exposed to:

flooding;

extreme heat;

storms;

water stress; and

other climate-related disruption.

These risks can affect airport operations, insurance costs and asset valuations.

Consequently, net-zero aviation finance involves both:

transition-risk management, concerning the movement toward a lower-carbon economy; and

physical-risk management, concerning direct effects of climate change.

11. Sustainable Finance Classification

A bank describing financing as “green” or “transition finance” must also consider the EU sustainable-finance framework.

Not every aviation investment automatically qualifies as environmentally sustainable.

A lender should distinguish between:

financing that genuinely reduces emissions;

ordinary aviation financing;

transitional investment;

environmentally sustainable activities satisfying relevant classification criteria; and

unsupported environmental marketing.

This distinction is important because misleading environmental claims can create regulatory and reputational risks.

12. Greenwashing

Suppose a bank provides €500 million to an airline and labels the entire facility “net-zero aviation finance,” even though only a small portion supports measurable transition activities.

Such claims may raise greenwashing concerns.

Credible transition finance therefore benefits from:

defined use of proceeds;

measurable objectives;

emissions methodology;

reporting;

verification where appropriate; and

transparent explanation of what the financing actually achieves.

“Net-zero” should therefore function as a measurable transition objective rather than merely a marketing label.

13. Sustainability-Linked Loans

Another mechanism is a sustainability-linked loan.

Unlike a traditional green loan, proceeds do not necessarily have to finance one designated environmental project.

Instead, financial terms can be linked to specified sustainability performance.

For an aviation borrower, relevant indicators might include objectively measurable matters concerning fuel efficiency, eligible SAF usage or emissions intensity.

However, the targets need to be sufficiently credible and meaningful.

Otherwise, the financing can create greenwashing rather than genuine transition incentives.

14. Aircraft Finance and Asset Risk

Aircraft are expensive assets and are frequently financed over long periods.

The net-zero transition creates an additional question:

Will today's aircraft remain economically competitive throughout the financing period?

A lender may need to consider:

expected fuel efficiency;

maintenance costs;

carbon costs;

future environmental requirements;

resale value; and

technological obsolescence.

An aircraft can therefore remain physically operational while becoming economically less attractive.

This is sometimes described as a form of stranded-asset risk.

15. State Aid

Government support for aviation transition can potentially fall within EU State-aid law.

Article 107 TFEU generally regulates advantages provided through State resources that selectively benefit undertakings and distort or threaten to distort competition.

Transition assistance may nevertheless be lawful where it falls within an applicable EU legal framework or is approved by the European Commission.

For banks, this matters when a financing structure depends upon:

government guarantees;

subsidies;

preferential loans;

recapitalisation;

airport support; or

other public financial advantages.

The legality and durability of that support can affect the bankability of the underlying transaction.

Relevant Case Law

There is no established judicial category called “Net-Zero Aviation Banking Law.”

The strongest relevant jurisprudence therefore comes from EU aviation, environmental and State-aid cases. These decisions establish principles affecting public financing, environmental regulation, airline support and the economic environment within which Spanish banks finance aviation.

16. Case 1: Ryanair v Commission (Spain; COVID-19) — Case T-628/20

Court: General Court of the European Union

Judgment: 19 May 2021

Spain established a €10 billion solvency-support fund for strategic undertakings facing temporary difficulties during the COVID-19 crisis.

Ryanair challenged the Commission's approval.

The General Court recognized that the Spanish measure constituted a State-aid scheme but upheld the relevant Commission approval, considering the scheme proportionate and compatible with the applicable framework.

Net-zero finance significance

The case demonstrates that large Spanish public financing programmes affecting strategic companies remain subject to EU State-aid controls.

The same principle matters where public resources are used to accelerate aviation transition.

17. Case 2: Ryanair v Commission — T-238/20

Court: General Court

Judgment: 17 February 2021

The case concerned a Swedish loan-guarantee scheme introduced for airlines during the COVID-19 crisis.

The litigation examined the compatibility of targeted aviation support with EU State-aid and non-discrimination principles.

Significance

Transition financing involving public guarantees must be structured within EU State-aid law.

A climate objective does not automatically exempt a financial measure from competition-law scrutiny.

18. Case 3: Ryanair v Commission (Finnair I) — T-388/20

Court: General Court

Judgment: 14 April 2021

The dispute concerned Finland's guarantee supporting a €600 million loan to Finnair.

The General Court upheld the relevant Commission decision authorising the measure.

Banking significance

This case directly demonstrates how bank-style financing and public guarantees interact in the aviation sector.

Similar legal analysis can become relevant where governments use guarantees or concessional mechanisms to mobilize private capital for aviation decarbonisation.

19. Case 4: Ryanair v Commission (SAS) — Cases T-378/20 and T-379/20

Court: General Court

Judgments: 14 April 2021

These proceedings concerned public support provided to SAS by Denmark and Sweden.

The General Court examined whether the measures complied with EU State-aid principles.

Transition-finance significance

The cases illustrate an important distinction:

policy justification does not eliminate State-aid analysis.

Future public financial support for low-carbon aircraft, SAF infrastructure or airline transition must similarly operate within applicable EU rules.

20. Case 5: Ryanair v Commission — T-643/20

This litigation formed part of the substantial body of EU cases concerning public aviation support.

The broader jurisprudence demonstrates that airline support measures can be challenged on grounds including:

selectivity;

proportionality;

discrimination;

competition effects; and

adequacy of the Commission's reasoning.

Banking significance

A commercial lender relying upon government support as part of a financing package should consider State-aid legal risk.

If a public measure is successfully challenged, the financial assumptions underlying the transaction can potentially change.

21. Case 6: Carpatair v Commission — T-522/20

Court: General Court

The litigation concerned measures involving Timișoara International Airport and Wizz Air, including airport charges and agreements governing airport infrastructure and services.

The dispute produced multiple stages of litigation concerning whether the relevant arrangements constituted State aid.

Following an appeal and referral, the General Court again addressed the dispute in May 2026 and annulled part of the Commission decision concerning the assessment of selectivity of airport charges.

Transition-finance significance

Airport decarbonisation will require substantial investment.

This case demonstrates that financial arrangements between publicly influenced airports and individual airlines can attract State-aid scrutiny.

Therefore, preferential charging arrangements designed to encourage environmental transition also need careful competition-law analysis.

22. Case 7: Commission and Others v Carpatair — Joined Cases C-244/23 P to C-246/23 P

Court: Court of Justice

Judgment: 13 February 2025

These appeals arose from the Carpatair litigation.

The Court of Justice set aside the earlier General Court judgment on issues relating to standing and referred the dispute back for further consideration. The General Court subsequently issued its 13 May 2026 judgment.

Banking significance

The extended litigation demonstrates the complexity and duration of State-aid disputes involving aviation infrastructure.

Banks financing airports or airlines should therefore consider legal uncertainty associated with public financial advantages rather than assuming that Commission approval or an initial judgment necessarily eliminates every future litigation risk.

23. What the Cases Establish

These cases do not create a special Spanish “net-zero aviation banking doctrine.”

Instead, they establish broader principles highly relevant to financing the transition.

Public financing is legally controlled. State-backed aviation support must comply with EU law.

Guarantees matter. Public guarantees can facilitate commercial borrowing but remain subject to State-aid analysis.

Competition matters. Environmental transition cannot automatically justify arbitrary preferential treatment.

Airport arrangements matter. Financial relationships between airports and airlines can themselves constitute potentially reviewable economic advantages.

Legal risk affects bankability. Long-running challenges to public support can alter the risk profile of financing transactions.

24. Role of Commercial Banks

Commercial banks can participate in the aviation transition through several channels:

Corporate loans for airlines and aerospace companies.

Project finance for SAF plants.

Syndicated loans for very large transition projects.

Asset finance for newer aircraft.

Sustainability-linked lending tied to measurable environmental targets.

Infrastructure finance for airports and fuel-distribution facilities.

Capital-market services supporting green or transition bonds.

Each structure requires separate analysis of credit, environmental and regulatory risks.

25. Blended Finance

Large aviation-transition projects may require blended finance.

For example:

Sponsor equity + commercial bank lending + EIB financing + qualifying public support.

The purpose is not simply to subsidize a project.

Public financing can sometimes address risks that private capital alone is unwilling to assume during the early development of new technologies.

Spain's EIB-supported Regional Resilience Fund already provides financial instruments supporting areas including clean transport and sustainable infrastructure.

The legal structure must nevertheless comply with banking, subsidy and State-aid requirements.

26. Financing Synthetic Aviation Fuel

Synthetic aviation fuel may create particularly significant financing requirements.

Production can require:

renewable electricity;

renewable hydrogen;

carbon inputs;

synthesis facilities;

refining;

storage;

transportation; and

long-term purchase agreements.

Banks financing such projects may therefore evaluate the entire supply chain.

The separate ReFuelEU synthetic-fuel requirement begins in 2030 and rises substantially toward 2050, creating an increasingly important regulatory driver for investment.

27. Long-Term Offtake Agreements

SAF plants require confidence that buyers will purchase their output.

Long-term offtake agreements between fuel producers and airlines can therefore become important to financing.

From a bank's perspective, a strong offtake agreement may provide greater certainty regarding future revenue.

However, lenders still need to consider:

airline creditworthiness;

fuel eligibility;

pricing formulas;

production risk;

regulatory change; and

termination rights.

A regulatory SAF mandate can support demand, but it does not eliminate commercial risk.

28. 2030 and 2050 Financing Horizon

Aviation transition finance is unusual because regulation establishes a long trajectory.

ReFuelEU requirements increase progressively through 2050.

This matters to banking because many investments made today will operate for decades.

A bank financing an aviation asset should therefore consider not merely today's regulatory requirements but reasonably foreseeable changes during the life of the financing.

Long-term transition planning becomes part of ordinary financial analysis.

29. Key Banking-Law Principles

The Spanish framework can ultimately be summarized through several principles.

Prudential soundness: A green purpose does not excuse poor credit underwriting.

Transition-risk assessment: Banks should consider how climate regulation affects borrowers and assets.

Credible environmental classification: Not every aviation loan is sustainable finance.

State-aid compliance: Public support must satisfy applicable EU requirements.

Technology neutrality within legal limits: Banks may finance different transition technologies where economically and legally viable.

Long-term assessment: Aircraft and infrastructure financing should consider regulatory developments over the asset's useful life.

Transparency: Environmental claims associated with financial products should accurately describe what the financing supports.

Blended finance: Commercial and public capital can operate together where the legal framework permits.

30. Conclusion

Banking Law and Net-Zero Aviation Transition in Spain is an emerging intersection of prudential banking regulation, aviation law, sustainable finance, environmental regulation and EU State-aid law.

The most important current regulatory driver is ReFuelEU Aviation (Regulation (EU) 2023/2405). It establishes progressively increasing sustainable aviation fuel requirements, beginning at 2% in 2025 and reaching 70% in 2050, together with increasing synthetic-fuel requirements from 2030.

The EU ETS adds another financial incentive by pricing aviation emissions, phasing out free aviation allowances and providing a mechanism using up to 20 million allowances during 2024–2030 to help address the price differential for eligible alternative aviation fuels.

Spanish and European financial institutions can support the transition through corporate loans, aircraft finance, SAF project finance, infrastructure lending, sustainability-linked facilities and public-private financing. EIB programmes demonstrate how financing can support clean transport and aerospace innovation, including major 2026 financing for aerospace R&D conducted partly in Spain.

Relevant case law—including Ryanair v Commission (Spain) T-628/20, Ryanair v Commission T-238/20, Finnair I T-388/20, the SAS cases T-378/20 and T-379/20, Carpatair T-522/20, and Commission and Others v Carpatair C-244/23 P to C-246/23 P—principally demonstrates how public aviation financing interacts with State-aid and competition law rather than establishing a distinct “net-zero banking” doctrine.

title: Mahasiswa Universitas Prasetiya Mulya Kembangkan Bioavtur dari Limbah Sawit
description:
Peluang tersebut menjadi fokus penelitian Gizky Dwi Andana, mahasiswa Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering (REE) Universitas Prasetiya Mulya angkatan 2021, yang berhasil mengembangkan katalis untuk mengolah Palm Fatty Acid Distillate (PFAD) menjadi bioavtur.
Di bawah bimbingan Peneliti BRIN Deliana Dahnum serta Kepala Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering Universitas Prasetiya Mulya Fidelis pengalaman tersebut memperkaya kompetensi sekaligus membangun portofolionya sebagai peneliti muda.
Karena itu kami membuka ruang kolaborasi dengan BRIN dan berbagai mitra agar pengalaman riset tidak berhenti di laboratorium kampus.
Melalui Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering (REE), Universitas Prasetiya Mulya, mahasiswa dibekali pengalaman belajar berbasis riset, proyek bersama industri, serta kolaborasi dengan lembaga penelitian nasional.
Informasi mengenai Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering, kurikulum, beasiswa, dan jalur penerimaan mahasiswa baru dapat diperoleh melalui https://www.prasetiyamulya.ac.id/program-s1/s1-renewable-energy-engineering/.
text:
Jakarta -

Di tengah upaya dunia mengembangkan Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) untuk mengurangi emisi karbon, Indonesia memiliki peluang besar memanfaatkan produk samping industri kelapa sawit sebagai bahan baku bioavtur. Peluang tersebut menjadi fokus penelitian Gizky Dwi Andana, mahasiswa Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering (REE) Universitas Prasetiya Mulya angkatan 2021, yang berhasil mengembangkan katalis untuk mengolah Palm Fatty Acid Distillate (PFAD) menjadi bioavtur.

Penelitian itu sekaligus mengantarkannya meraih Global Korea Scholarship (GKS), beasiswa penuh dari Pemerintah Korea Selatan untuk melanjutkan studi magister di Gyeongsang National University.

Riset yang dilakukan Gizky menjawab tantangan global untuk menghasilkan bahan bakar penerbangan yang lebih ramah lingkungan sekaligus meningkatkan nilai tambah produk samping industri sawit. Melalui pemanfaatan PFAD sebagai bahan baku, ia mengembangkan katalis berbasis metal-organic framework (MOF) ZIF-67 untuk mempercepat proses konversi menjadi bioavtur.

Hasil pengujian menunjukkan tingkat konversi PFAD di atas 99 persen dengan selektivitas bioavtur mendekati 80 persen. Angka tersebut menunjukkan efisiensi proses yang sangat tinggi sehingga berpotensi mendukung pengembangan teknologi produksi bioavtur yang lebih efektif.

Inovasi ini juga tengah memasuki proses pengajuan paten bersama tim peneliti Badan Riset dan Inovasi Nasional (BRIN) sebagai bagian dari upaya hilirisasi hasil riset menuju pemanfaatan yang lebih luas.

Katalis 1:1, katalis ini dibuat dengan menggunakan nikel dan tembaga dalam jumlah yang sama. Secara keseluruhan, kedua logam tersebut menyumbang 10% dari komposisi katalis.

Gizky mengatakan penelitian tersebut berawal dari keinginan memanfaatkan potensi yang selama ini belum dimaksimalkan.

"Indonesia merupakan salah satu produsen kelapa sawit terbesar di dunia. Saya melihat masih banyak produk samping yang belum dimanfaatkan secara optimal. Saya percaya limbah bukan berarti tidak berguna. Tantangannya adalah menemukan cara agar limbah itu memiliki nilai dan memberi manfaat yang lebih besar," kata Gizky dalam keterangan tertulis, Senin (28/9/2026).

Perjalanan riset itu juga menunjukkan bagaimana mahasiswa dapat terlibat langsung dalam penelitian berskala nasional sejak masih kuliah. Sebagai asisten peneliti di BRIN, Gizky terlibat dalam berbagai tahapan penelitian, mulai dari sintesis material katalis, pengujian laboratorium, hingga pengembangan teknologi yang berpotensi diterapkan di sektor energi.

Di bawah bimbingan Peneliti BRIN Deliana Dahnum serta Kepala Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering Universitas Prasetiya Mulya Fidelis pengalaman tersebut memperkaya kompetensi sekaligus membangun portofolionya sebagai peneliti muda. Pengalaman itu menjadi salah satu bekal yang mengantarkannya meraih beasiswa penuh untuk melanjutkan studi di Korea Selatan.

Menurut Fidelis, pengalaman riset menjadi bagian penting dari proses pembelajaran di Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering karena mahasiswa tidak hanya mempelajari teori, tetapi juga dibiasakan menyelesaikan persoalan nyata melalui pendekatan ilmiah.

"Mahasiswa akan belajar jauh lebih cepat ketika mereka diberi kesempatan menyelesaikan persoalan nyata. Karena itu kami membuka ruang kolaborasi dengan BRIN dan berbagai mitra agar pengalaman riset tidak berhenti di laboratorium kampus. Perjalanan Gizky menunjukkan bagaimana pembelajaran, riset, dan kolaborasi dapat melahirkan inovasi yang bermanfaat sekaligus membuka peluang di tingkat global," kata Fidelis.

Di Gyeongsang National University, Gizky berencana melanjutkan penelitian menggunakan material berbasis ZIF-67 untuk aplikasi penangkapan karbon dioksida (CO₂), teknologi yang diharapkan dapat mendukung upaya pengurangan emisi gas rumah kaca.

Perjalanan Gizky memperlihatkan bahwa karir di bidang energi bersih dapat dibangun sejak di bangku kuliah melalui pengalaman riset, kolaborasi dengan industri, dan keterlibatan dalam proyek-proyek strategis. Seiring meningkatnya investasi pada sektor energi terbarukan, dekarbonisasi industri, dan teknologi keberlanjutan, kebutuhan terhadap talenta di bidang rekayasa energi juga terus bertumbuh.

Melalui Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering (REE), Universitas Prasetiya Mulya, mahasiswa dibekali pengalaman belajar berbasis riset, proyek bersama industri, serta kolaborasi dengan lembaga penelitian nasional. Pendekatan tersebut membuka peluang karier di berbagai sektor, mulai dari energi terbarukan, manufaktur, minyak dan gas, teknologi, konsultan keberlanjutan, lembaga riset, hingga perusahaan yang menjalankan transformasi menuju energi bersih. Lulusan juga memiliki kesempatan melanjutkan studi di berbagai universitas terkemuka dunia.

"Bagi generasi muda yang ingin berkontribusi dalam pengembangan energi bersih dan teknologi berkelanjutan, Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering (REE) Universitas Prasetiya Mulya menawarkan lingkungan belajar yang menghubungkan ruang kelas, laboratorium riset, dan dunia industri. Pengalaman seperti yang dijalani Gizky menunjukkan bahwa langkah menuju karir di sektor energi masa depan dapat dimulai sejak menjadi mahasiswa," tutup Fidelis.

Informasi mengenai Program Studi Renewable Energy Engineering, kurikulum, beasiswa, dan jalur penerimaan mahasiswa baru dapat diperoleh melalui https://www.prasetiyamulya.ac.id/program-s1/s1-renewable-energy-engineering/.

text:
Nine red jets pull up in front of the crowd, and on a word from the leader, "Smoke on, go," thick white trails pour from their tails. Seconds later, red and blue join the white, and the Union Flag is painted across the sky.

Display smoke is the simplest trick at any airshow, and the one people ask about most. It is not a special exhaust or a burning fuel leak. It is oil, sprayed into a very hot place at exactly the right moment. Here is how the world's best-known teams do it, and why they bother.

Oil Into Fire

Every display smoke system works on the same idea. A tank carries a light oil. A pump pushes it through injectors into the jet pipe or exhaust, where temperatures are hundreds of degrees. The oil vaporises in an instant, and as the vapour hits the cold air behind the aircraft it condenses into billions of tiny droplets. That is the white trail: not combustion smoke, but an aerosol, much like a cloud.

The US Navy's Blue Angels describe the process in one sentence in their official FAQ, and it applies almost word for word to every jet team.

How the Colours Are Made

White is the natural colour. Red, blue or green come from dye mixed into the oil before it is injected. On the Red Arrows' Hawks, the smoke system sits in a pod under the fuselage, carrying diesel-based fluid; plain fluid makes white smoke, and dyed fluid makes red and blue. Pilots trigger each colour from a button in the cockpit, which is how the team can switch colours in the blink of an eye.

The Frecce Tricolori, the Italian Air Force team formed in 1961 and flying the Aermacchi MB-339, do the same with green, white and red. Their signature finish, a ten-aircraft pass trailing the Italian tricolour, is one of the best-known images in display flying.

Why Teams Use Smoke

For the crowd, smoke turns a fast, small aircraft into a line you can follow. A loop becomes a circle drawn in the sky; a crossing becomes a visible X. Without it, much of a display would be a series of dots.

For the pilots, it is a safety tool. The Blue Angels say smoke helps their solo pilots see each other during opposing manoeuvres, when two jets race towards each other head-on and must pass at precise distances. A smoke trail makes the other aircraft far easier to pick up against a cluttered horizon.

Greener Smoke

Diesel works, but it is dirty and can stain paint. Teams have been moving to cleaner fluids. In 2025 the Red Arrows flew their Royal International Air Tattoo displays on sustainable aviation fuel for the first time, and switched the smoke pod from diesel to a biofuel based on vegetable oil, according to the RAF and The Aviationist.

Whatever is in the tank, the effect is the same: a few litres of oil and a hot jet pipe produce the most photographed thing at any airshow.

Sources: U.S. Navy Blue Angels FAQ; Royal Air Force Red Arrows team information; RAFRedArrows.co.uk; The Aviationist (July 2025); Wikipedia (Frecce Tricolori).

text:
Clean fuels are shifting from a policy ambition to an industrial reality in North America, and for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) producers in Canada, scaling alternative feedstocks and production pathways presents an opportunity to help reach domestic SAF targets.

Speaking on a recent gasworld webinar, Seth Brouwers, Chief Innovation Officer at Canadian clean technology firm Sustaero, said, “Having a secure energy supply [and] producing our own fuels using our own resources is a huge opportunity and can be a huge strength.”

This energy and feedstock reliability, paired with government support, plays a key role in de-risking projects and investment, he added.

Accelerating domestic SAF project investment and scaling up supply is key to meeting Canada’s Aviation Climate Action Plan target of 10% SAF use by 2030.

Sustaero is one company in this space and converts sustainable biomass into SAF through a proven syngas-to-liquids pathway.

In July, Sustaero selected Danish firm Topsoe and South African chemical and energy company Sasol as the technology providers for the Sustaero SAF project in northern Ontario, Canada.

Once fully operational in 2030, the facility is expected to produce 3,200 barrels per day of SAF with expansion potential of three times initial capacity.

Other elements of project de-risking, and key challenges for scaling SAF production, include securing reliable technology, long-term feedstock security, and sourcing low-carbon reliable electricity, Brouwers noted.

“We need woody biomass SAF…so absolutely, the opportunity is scalable, and we see biomass to liquids being a critical pathway to achieve these targets,” he said.

This coincides with a report from the Canadian Council for Sustainable Aviation Fuels (C-SAF), which states that Canada has enough sustainable biomass to produce seven to ten billion litres of SAF a year.

This amount, if used in aviation, is what Canada would need to meet aviation fuel demand in 2030, representing an opportunity to scale up the domestic SAF market.

title: US SAF Market Faces Policy Uncertainty as AtJ and PtL Scale - Bioenergy Business

text:
The US sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market is entering a period of technological expansion alongside changes to federal incentives, with alcohol-to-jet (AtJ) and power-to-liquid (PtL) projects emerging as important pathways for future production.

Research firm IDTechEx expects new SAF technologies and production facilities to influence the US market over the coming decade, while the economics of projects will remain closely linked to feedstock, renewable power and policy conditions.

The policy landscape changed significantly with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted in July 2025. Under amendments to the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit, the special higher credit rate for SAF was removed for fuel produced after December 31, 2025. Eligible transportation fuel produced after that date can receive a base credit of $0.20 per gallon or an alternative amount of $1 per gallon when prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements are met, subject to emissions-factor and other requirements.

The legislation also extended Section 45Z through the end of 2029 and introduced restrictions on eligible feedstocks and certain foreign entities.

AtJ technology moves into commercial production

One of the technologies gaining commercial-scale experience in the US is alcohol-to-jet, which converts alcohol feedstocks such as ethanol into jet fuel.

LanzaJet’s Freedom Pines Fuels facility in Soperton, Georgia, is designed to produce up to 10 million gallons of sustainable fuels annually. The facility is the world’s first commercial ethanol-to-SAF plant and is designed to produce around nine million gallons of SAF and one million gallons of renewable diesel in its initial operating configuration.

The facility uses LanzaJet’s ATJ process together with Technip Energies’ Hummingbird technology. The latter is integrated into the process for converting ethanol-derived intermediates into products suitable for fuel production.

The project provides a commercial reference point for the wider deployment of AtJ technology, while also demonstrating the importance of ethanol supply to the economics of the pathway.

LanzaJet has said Freedom Pines will source low-carbon ethanol, including ethanol from waste-based feedstocks. The company also has offtake agreements in place and has positioned the facility as a platform for scaling its technology to other markets.

Infinium advances PtL SAF production in Texas

A different production model is being developed by Infinium through Project Roadrunner in West Texas.

The project will use renewable electricity, captured carbon dioxide and green hydrogen to manufacture synthetic fuels, primarily eSAF, alongside e-diesel and e-naphtha. Infinium expects Roadrunner to produce approximately 23,000 tonnes per year, or about 7.6 million gallons, of combined eSAF and other e-fuel products once operational. Commercial operations are expected in 2027.

Roadrunner has secured 150 MW of new wind generation capacity through a long-term power purchase agreement with a subsidiary of NextEra Energy Resources. The project is also using a 100 MW electrolyser system to produce hydrogen for the PtL process.

Infinium reached final investment decision on Roadrunner in 2025, with Brookfield Asset Management and Breakthrough Energy Catalyst among the project investors. HSBC subsequently provided project-based financing. Long-term offtake agreements have also been secured with American Airlines and International Airlines Group.

Feedstock and power costs remain central to SAF economics

The emergence of AtJ and PtL provides the US market with different routes towards SAF production, but the two pathways face different economic constraints.

AtJ projects depend on reliable supplies of suitable low-carbon alcohol feedstocks, particularly ethanol. Feedstock availability, carbon intensity and pricing can therefore influence the cost and emissions performance of the resulting SAF.

PtL projects face a different cost structure. They require substantial quantities of renewable electricity to produce hydrogen through electrolysis, as well as a suitable source of carbon dioxide.

Roadrunner illustrates this integration by combining dedicated renewable electricity, electrolysis, captured CO₂ and fuel synthesis within one production system.

As US electricity generation capacity expands, access to competitively priced renewable power could become increasingly important for e-fuel economics. However, the cost of electricity, electrolyser utilisation, hydrogen production, CO₂ sourcing and downstream conversion will all influence the competitiveness of PtL SAF.

Policy will remain a major factor

The changing Section 45Z framework adds another variable to project economics.

The current credit is available for qualifying clean transportation fuel produced and sold through December 31, 2029. For fuel produced after December 31, 2025, the SAF-specific higher credit amounts no longer apply, while the remaining credit is linked to the applicable amount, emissions factor and prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements. Eligible fuels must also meet new feedstock-origin requirements.

This means SAF developers must assess projects against both technology and policy conditions over long investment horizons.

For first-of-a-kind facilities, the ability to secure long-term offtake agreements, project financing, feedstock supplies and renewable power can be particularly important to reducing commercial risk. Roadrunner, for example, has combined project equity, debt financing, dedicated wind capacity and long-term airline offtake arrangements.

Bioenergy Business Analysis

The US SAF market is increasingly moving beyond a single technology pathway. AtJ provides a route for converting established alcohol feedstocks into aviation fuel, while PtL can produce synthetic aviation fuels from renewable electricity, hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide.

The commercial performance of these pathways will depend on more than technology readiness. Feedstock and electricity costs, carbon intensity, plant utilisation, financing structures, offtake agreements and the durability of federal policy incentives will all influence project economics.

The policy changes to Section 45Z therefore arrive at a significant stage for the US SAF industry. Projects such as Freedom Pines and Roadrunner provide commercial-scale demonstrations of different production models, but their longer-term competitiveness will depend on how technology costs develop alongside the US feedstock, electricity and regulatory environment.

For SAF producers and investors, the next phase of the market is likely to be defined by the interaction between technology choice, feedstock economics, renewable power availability and policy support, rather than by a single dominant production pathway.

title: Egypt SAF Policies: CAA Calls for Practical Approach - Bioenergy Business
